prerequisites: Good knowledge of real and complex variable calculus
Good knowledge of functional analysis (representation and operations with real and complex variable functions)

learning_outcomes.text: Students have demonstrated possession and understanding of knowledge in a field of study that builds on general secondary education, and is typically at a level that, while supported by advanced textbooks, also includes some aspects that involve knowledge from the forefront of their field of study.

Students are able to apply their knowledge to their work or vocation in a professional manner and possess the competencies typically demonstrated by the formulation and defense of arguments and the solution of problems within their field of study.
Students have the ability to gather and interpret relevant data (usually within their field of study) to make judgments that include a reflection on relevant social, scientific, or ethical issues.
Students can transmit information, ideas, problems, and solutions to both specialized and non-specialized audiences.
Students have developed the learning skills necessary to undertake further studies with a high degree of autonomy.

Choose and apply the most appropriate methods and techniques to analyze and solve problems defined by data that represent a challenge due to their volume, velocity, variety, or heterogeneity, including computational, mathematical, statistical, and signal processing methods.

Possess experimental and analytical skills to work autonomously, being able to design experiments and describe, analyze, evaluate, and interpret the resulting information to propose alternative and novel solutions to known and/or emerging problems.
Create models and make decisions based on available data, combining acquired knowledge and being able to apply new knowledge to problem-solving.
Ability to integrate into a multidisciplinary team within the framework of a data science project.
Ability to access and manage information in different formats for subsequent analysis in order to obtain knowledge from data.
Ability to express data processing results clearly and convincingly, both in writing and orally.
Understanding and mastery of the basic concepts of information, signal, and system theory, used in different schemes and techniques for data representation and manipulation.
Ability to analyze, encode, process, and transmit information and data using signal processing techniques.
Be able to represent a signal from samples and reconstruct a signal from its samples.
Be able to characterize signals and data in different domains (temporal, frequency, spatial, etc.), and know how to transform between these domains.
Ability to evaluate the advantages and disadvantages of different implementation alternatives for information processing systems, from the point of view of signal space, perturbations, and noise.
Ability to have a global vision of a complex signal and data processing system and the interactions between its components.

Understand the concept of analog and digital signals and data. Handle sampling, interpolation, quantization operations, and associated theorems and transformations (Fourier series expansion, Fourier transform, Laplace transform, and Z transform).
Be able to apply signal and system concepts to solve dimensionality reduction problems in data sets.
Be able to apply signal and system concepts to select the most suitable space for data treatment, as well as to represent and operate with data in that space.

syllabus_topics: Relationship between algebra/calculus and signal and system theory
Review of vector spaces and particularization of signal spaces
Definition of the Dirac delta and physical meaning
Relationship of the Dirac delta with the step function
Operations with distributions (derivatives, convolutions, product, and system resolution)
Definition of the Fourier series expansion (FSE)
Relationship of the FSE with linear and invariant systems
Relationship between the FT and linear and invariant systems
Definition of the FSE for discrete variable signals
Convergence of the FSE for discrete variable signals
Properties of the FSE for discrete variable signals
Examples of the FSE for discrete variable signals
Relationship of FSE with linear and invariant systems
Definition of the FT for discrete variable signals
Convergence of the FT for discrete variable signals
Properties of the FT for discrete variable signals
Examples of the FT for discrete variable signals
Relationship of the FT with linear and invariant systems
Sampling and recovery of continuous variable signals
Modeling a continuous LTI system using a discrete LTI system
teaching_methods: Asynchronous non-presential activities (theoretical content, problem-solving, exercises, IT tools)

assessment_methods.method: Active Participation in Forums and Virtual Campus Activities [CV]

assessment_rules: For the ordinary call, the final grade is calculated as: PS * 0.05 + CV * D * 0.1 + ET * 0.4 + EP * 0.45, where PS, CV, ET, and EP are on a scale of 0 to 10, and D is binary (0 or 1) from a complementary oral defense. Grades obtained in the ordinary call are not valid for other calls. For extraordinary calls, the final grade is ET * 0.5 + EP * 0.5. Students with differentiated evaluation will be assessed according to the extraordinary call system.
